outcome: The unstable conjecture is still open and no counterexample to it is claimed. Since 26 January 2024 the events are: computer-assisted unstable trivializations of Miller-Schupp family instances (a NeurIPS 2025 paper reporting 753 presentations solved across all runs, and a June 2026 ICML paper reporting over 100 newly trivialized benchmark presentations); reductions of Akbulut-Kirby (AK) and Miller-Schupp presentations to AK(3) or to each other; a 2024 preprint whose claim that AK(3) is stably trivial was withdrawn from its v2 abstract and is contested; an independent 2025 proof of stable AC-equivalence of AK(3) to the trivial presentation; a partial stable-version result via fake surfaces; and a June 2026 unstable proof restricted to thickenable presentations.
problem_asks: Read from the statement alone: (1) for every number n of generators, every balanced presentation of the trivial group, i.e. n generators with n relators whose group is trivial; (2) each such presentation can be transformed into the trivial presentation (n generators, relators equal to the generators); (3) using only Nielsen transformations on the relators (replacing a relator by its product with another relator, or by its inverse) and conjugations of relators, with no addition or removal of generators or relators. The question is the truth of this universal yes/no claim. The bullet names no other quantity, and asks nothing about stabilised or cyclic variants.

events.what_happened: A. D. Miasnikov and A. G. Myasnikov, 'Balanced presentations of the trivial group on two generators and the Andrews-Curtis conjecture' (arXiv math/0304305), describe all balanced two-generator presentations of the trivial group with total relator length at most 12 and show that all of them satisfy the conjecture.
events.delivers: Finite census: every two-generator balanced presentation of the trivial group with total relator length at most 12 is AC-trivializable (unstable moves, as stated in the abstract).
events.remains: Every presentation of total relator length 13 or more, every rank other than 2, and the conjecture as a universal claim.
events.directly_checkable: Each presentation of total relator length at most 12 can be checked by replaying its trivializing move sequence; the paper's own computations were not inspected.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for a finite list of cases; the list does not change the universal claim.

events.what_happened: M. R. Bridson, 'The complexity of balanced presentations and the Andrews-Curtis conjecture' (arXiv 1504.04187, 16 April 2015), proves large lower bounds on the number of Andrews-Curtis moves needed to trivialise certain balanced presentations of the trivial group, beginning in rank 4.
events.delivers: Lower bounds on the length of AC-trivialisations for a family of rank-4 and higher balanced presentations of the trivial group; the presentations are constructed from groups with deficiency-1 presentations and are trivial exactly when a given word is trivial in that group.
events.remains: Whether these presentations are AC-trivializable at all (the bounds are on move counts, and are stated to be finite), and the conjecture as a whole.
events.direction: Bears on computer searches: the author warns that failure of a search to find a trivialising sequence is weak evidence. Does not answer the universal claim.

events.what_happened: S. V. Ivanov, 'On conjectures of Andrews and Curtis' (arXiv 1606.08196, 27 June 2016; published in Proc. AMS 146 (2018), 2283-2298, not opened). The abstract states that the original conjecture is equivalent to a cyclic version in which only cyclic permutations replace arbitrary conjugations.
events.revisions: Single arXiv version (v1). Journal version Proc. AMS 146 (2018) per search listing, not opened.
events.delivers: A reduction: the unstable conjecture is equivalent to its cyclic-permutation version. For the variant without stabilisations, the abstract says the restriction makes the conjecture false.
events.remains: The conjecture itself is neither proved nor disproved; the equivalence is a reformulation.

checked_by.who: Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in volume 146 (2018) per the AMS listing; the referee process was not inspected

events.direction: Reformulation; cuts neither way on the universal claim as stated.

events.what_happened: W. Metzler, 'On the generalized Andrews-Curtis-Problem - A Disproof of the Relative Case' (arXiv 2102.03212, v1 5 Feb 2021). The claimed disproof concerns finite PLCW 2-complexes that are simple-homotopy equivalent and must be deformed into each other with fixed subcomplexes. v3 (23 Feb 2021) is withdrawn by the author.
events.revisions: v2 15 Feb 2021; v3 23 Feb 2021 marked withdrawn by the author. The v1 and v2 PDFs are 6 KB each; no withdrawal reason is given on the page.
events.delivers: Claimed to show that the generalized (complex-level) version fails when subcomplexes are held fixed. The comment field says the theorem and proof speak only of Q*-equivalences and that it is not clear whether this excludes the relative (AC') counterexamples.
events.remains: The unstable conjecture for presentations of the trivial group is untouched; the generalized and relative versions are different questions.
events.doubts: The author's own comment field records an unresolved scope gap (Q*-equivalences only, and unclear whether relative counterexamples are excluded). The paper was withdrawn about two weeks after first posting.

withdrawn.what: arXiv v3 of 2102.03212 withdrawn by the author; no reason given on the arXiv page

events.direction: Claimed to cut against the relative/generalized version; withdrawn; does not address the unstable trivial-group question.

events.what_happened: N. Bagherifard and E. Eftekhary, 'Simple balanced three-manifolds, Heegaard Floer homology and the Andrews-Curtis conjecture' (arXiv 2205.14706, 29 May 2022; v2 2 June 2022 minor corrections; published Algebraic & Geometric Topology 24(8), December 2024 per the search listing). The abstract uses Heegaard Floer homology to show that some simple balanced 3-manifolds are not in the trivial equivalence class, motivated by an analogy with Andrews-Curtis equivalence.
events.revisions: v2 2 Jun 2022 ('minor (non-mathematical) corrections'). Journal version AGT 24(8), Dec 2024 (the journal PDF was not text-readable, so the publication date is from the search listing).
events.delivers: A result about a 3-manifold analogue of Andrews-Curtis equivalence (simple balanced 3-manifolds not equivalent to S^2 x [-1,1]). It is not a statement about group presentations.
events.remains: The group-theoretic conjecture as stated is not addressed.
events.direction: Analogue only. The abstract motivates the work by the conjecture but does not say the group conjecture is false.
events.object: Simple balanced 3-manifolds not in the trivial equivalence class; the authors use Heegaard Floer tools to prove this, so the object is non-constructive in the sense that it is an existence proof from the invariant.

events.what_happened: A. Shehper, A. Medina-Mardones, L. Fagan, B. Lewandowski, A. Gruen, Y. Qiu, P. Kucharski, Z. Wang, S. Gukov, 'What makes math problems hard for reinforcement learning: a case study' (arXiv 2408.15332, v1 27 Aug 2024; v2 11 Feb 2025). v1 abstract: the authors 'demonstrate that one of the potential counterexamples due to Akbulut and Kirby, whose status escaped direct mathematical methods for 39 years, is stably AC-trivial'. v2 abstract, read directly: length reducibility of all but two presentations in the Akbulut-Kirby series (1981), and resolution of various potential counterexamples in the Miller-Schupp series (1991), including three infinite subfamilies. The v2 introduction says 'we also found AC-trivializations of hundreds of Miller-Schupp presentations' and 'we apply reinforcement learning to demonstrate its AC equivalence to AK(3)'. v2 Section 2 says 'the presentation MS(3,w1) of length 15 is AC-equivalent to AK(3)', and Section 3.3 says four presentations 'are AC-equivalent to AK(3)'. v2 Section 2 says the AK(3) trivialization attempts by breadth-first search failed and calls AK(3) a potential counterexample.
events.revisions: v1 27 Aug 2024 abstract claims stable AC-triviality of an Akbulut-Kirby candidate (the abstract does not name it; the 39-year gap matches AK(3)). v2 11 Feb 2025: the abstract no longer contains that claim; the v2 introduction says 'we discovered a subtle misprint in [MMS02, p.10] that had gone unnoticed for more than 20 years. This misprint undermines the claim that (1) is stably AC-trivial', where (1) is a presentation from the 2002 paper and the paper says (1) is AC-equivalent to AK(3). Appendix F ('A misprint in the Wirtinger presentation of [MMS02]') is listed but was not readable. v2 Section 9 calls AK(3) 'a potential counterexample for the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture'. I did not see an explicit retraction sentence and did not see a changelog.
events.delivers: Unstable, restricted to the Akbulut-Kirby series and Miller-Schupp families: length reduction for the AK series (all but two presentations); AC-equivalences of several Miller-Schupp presentations to AK(3) (including a length-15 example and four presentations per Section 3.3); unstable trivializations of hundreds of Miller-Schupp presentations and of three infinite subfamilies of potential counterexamples (abstract; instance-level, not a proof for the full families as far as I read). The v1 stable-triviality claim for an AK-type candidate is not delivered in v2 and is in any case about the stable question.
events.remains: The unstable conjecture for AK(n) with n of at least 3 (AK(3) is stated open in v2 Section 2 and in the Two-Hump paper); the unstable status of all Miller-Schupp presentations not listed; the stable question, where v2 says AK(3) remains a potential counterexample.

checked_by.who: Alexei Lisitsa (University of Liverpool), automated-deduction group
checked_by.qualification: Researcher on automated reasoning applied to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture, with prior published papers on it

checked_by.qualification: Author of the 2026 paper that supplies explicit move sequences for AK(3) equivalences
checked_by.what_they_did: States that the two AK(3)-equivalences for MS(3,...) presentations are 'the first public explicit certificates' for equivalences that Shehper et al. stated without proof; provides a replayable verifier

events.directly_checkable: The AK(3)-equivalence claims for MS(3,...) presentations: Carreras's sequences (66 and 13 moves) are a public check of two of the four claimed equivalences; the other two claimed equivalences have no published sequence in the sources read.
events.doubts: (a) The v1 stable-triviality claim is undermined by the authors' own v2 misprint note concerning MMS02 presentation (1). (b) The four AK(3)-equivalence claims were, per Carreras, stated without move sequences; two have now been certified by a third party, two not in the sources read. (c) The v2 full text was read only through about the first 100,000 of 218,000 characters plus Section 9's opening, so the Miller-Schupp trivialization claims and the 'three infinite subfamilies' were not checked against the body.
events.direction: Unstable: reductions and equivalences to AK(3) and length reductions for the AK series; trivializations of many specific Miller-Schupp presentations; no counterexample. Stable (v1 only): claim that an AK-type candidate is stably trivial, which v2 withdraws in effect.
events.object: Not an object in the sense of a counterexample. The AK series presentations AK(n) (two generators, relators a^n b^-(n+1) and abab^-1a^-1b^-1) are reduced to shorter AC-equivalent presentations; a length-14 presentation AC-equivalent to AK(3) and the MS(3,...) presentations are cited as equivalent to AK(3).

systems.name: reinforcement learning agent
systems.what_it_did: Searched for AC-trivializing move sequences; the authors say it solved two hard presentations that classical search could not, and produced AC-trivializations of hundreds of Miller-Schupp presentations. The v2 text says reinforcement learning was applied to demonstrate AC equivalence of a presentation to AK(3). The paper does not name a model or a library.
systems.basis_quote: we apply reinforcement learning to demonstrate its AC equivalence to AK(3).

events.what_happened: A. Lisitsa, 'Towards computer-assisted proofs of parametric Andrews-Curtis simplifications, II' (EasyChair Preprint 13320, 16 May 2024). The abstract says automated theorem proving yields previously unknown simplifications of presentations from the parametric family MS_n(w*) for n = 3,...,7, and formulates two conjectures on the structure of simplifications for n of at least 3. The journal version 'New Andrews-Curtis trivializations for Miller-Schupp group presentations' (Examples and Counterexamples 6, article 100168, Dec 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.exco.2024.100168) extends to n = 3,...,8 according to the search listing; the journal article was not readable.
events.revisions: Preprint covers n = 3..7; journal version (Dec 2024) covers n = 3..8 per the search listing (not opened). Earlier conference version at AITP 2023 as an abstract.
events.delivers: Unstable (term-rewriting, first-order automated reasoning) AC-simplifications of MS_n(w*) for specific n in 3..7 (preprint) or 3..8 (journal). Instance-level for each stated n.
events.remains: The infinite family MS_n(w*) for all n of at least 3 (the paper formulates conjectures about it), all other families, and the AK series.

machine_checked.system: Automated theorem prover output (classical first-order reasoning; the preprint describes the method as automated theorem proving and does not name a prover)

events.directly_checkable: The simplification sequences, if provided in the paper; not inspected.
events.direction: Unstable instance-level trivializations; does not touch the universal claim beyond the instances it lists.

events.what_happened: A. Lisitsa, 'Stable Andrews-Curtis trivialization of AK(3) revisited. A case study using automated deduction' (arXiv 2501.18601, 17 January 2025, one version). Gives an alternative proof, using the Prover9 automated theorem prover, that AK(3) is stably AC-equivalent to the trivial presentation, and gives transformation sequences from two Prover9 proofs. The abstract credits the result to Shehper et al. (2024).
events.delivers: Stable form only: AK(3) is stably AC-equivalent to the trivial presentation, certified by the sequences given. It does not claim the unstable conjecture holds for AK(3).
events.remains: The unstable question for AK(3) (the abstract does not address it); the unstable conjecture generally; the stable conjecture for other presentations.

machine_checked.system: Prover9 (automated theorem prover); the paper provides transformation sequences derived from its proofs

events.directly_checkable: The transformation sequences in the paper: a stable AC-equivalence between AK(3) and the trivial presentation that a reader can replay by hand or with a small script. Not replayed here.
events.doubts: The stable claim it independently re-derives is attributed to Shehper et al. (2024), whose v2 now treats the related presentation (1) as undermined by a misprint. Whether the sequences given here are correct was not checked.
events.direction: Stable form: cuts toward triviality of AK(3) in the stable setting. Unstable form: unaddressed.
events.object: Transformation sequences deriving the stable AC-equivalence of the AK(3) presentation with the trivial presentation; the object is a sequence of moves that can be replayed to check the equivalence.

events.what_happened: L. Fagan, Y. Qiu, Z. Wang, 'Stable Andrews-Curtis Conjecture via Fake Surfaces and Zeeman Conjecture' (arXiv 2412.12293, v1 16 Dec 2024; v2 8 Jan 2026). The abstract proposes an induction scheme 'that aims at establishing the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture in the affirmative' and states that the stable conjecture is equivalent to the claim that every contractible fake surface is 3-deformable to a point. It proves this for contractible fake surfaces of complexity less than 6, by induction.
events.revisions: v2 8 Jan 2026; I did not compare v1 and v2 text.
events.delivers: Stable form only: reduces the stable conjecture to the fake-surface statement and proves that statement for complexity less than 6. The abstract does not claim the stable conjecture is proved.
events.remains: The stable conjecture for complexity 6 and above, and the unstable conjecture in full.
events.time_since_posted: about 22 months (Dec 2024 to Oct 2026) with no published engagement found; the v2 of Jan 2026 is the only later sign
events.direction: Stable form: partial progress toward the stable conjecture; no counterexample; does not touch the unstable statement.

events.what_happened: J. A. Barmak, 'An exotic presentation of Z x Z and the Andrews-Curtis conjecture', Algebraic & Geometric Topology 25(1) (2025), 345-355. Per the search extract of the journal page, it shows that two two-generator presentations of Z x Z, with simple-homotopy-equivalent standard complexes, are not Q*-equivalent, using a winding invariant. The journal page I opened did not show the abstract, so this rests on the search extract.
events.revisions: No arXiv preprint located. The journal publication is 5 March 2025 (search listing). I have not dated it to the journal, because the rule is the first public written argument; none earlier was found, so the year is the best available.
events.delivers: Concerns presentations of Z x Z (not the trivial group) and a generalised equivalence relation (Q*, simple-homotopy version). It shows the generalised relation distinguishes two presentations; it does not touch the trivial-group statement.
events.remains: The trivial-group conjecture as stated, which is not in its scope.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper in volume 25, issue 1 (2025); the referee process was not inspected

events.directly_checkable: The two presentations of Z x Z can be compared by hand in the paper; not inspected.
events.doubts: Scope: the object is a presentation of Z x Z under a generalised relation, so it is a different question from the trivial-group conjecture as stated, which I record here for the judging pass.
events.direction: Cuts against a generalised version (simple-homotopy-equivalent presentations need not be Q*-equivalent); says nothing about the trivial-group presentations.
events.object: Two presentations of Z x Z, each with two generators and two relators, whose standard complexes are simple-homotopy equivalent but which are not Q*-equivalent; the separating invariant is the winding invariant. The explicit pair is not reproduced here.

events.what_happened: N. Bagherifard, with E. Eftekhary, gave a talk 'A 3-dimensional approach to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture'. The Oregon State seminar listing (12 May 2025, opened only via search snippet) and the Georgia Tech Topology Techtalk (6 Dec 2025, opened) carry the abstract. It says the talk will 'explain a partial connection between the Andrews-Curtis equivalence and a notion of equivalence on certain families of 3-manifolds, and ... demonstrate that a version of the conjecture is not true.'
events.revisions: Same abstract at Georgia Tech on 6 Dec 2025. No written argument (preprint or paper) located for the 'not true' claim.
events.delivers: Per the abstract only: a version of the conjecture is false, obtained through the 3-manifold equivalence. The version is not named in the abstract.
events.remains: Unknown from the abstract: which version is meant. It may be the 3-manifold analogue of the 2022 paper, or a different statement.
events.time_since_posted: about 17 months from the first talk abstract (May 2025 to Oct 2026) with no written argument found
events.doubts: Abstract only. The abstract itself also says 'some believe both conjectures may be incorrect' and speaks of demonstrating in the talk. The 2022 paper by the same first author is about the 3-manifold analogue and does not state a disproof of the group conjecture. No preprint located.
events.direction: Claimed to cut against 'a version' of the conjecture; which version is unspecified; no written argument.

events.what_happened: R. H. Gilman and A. G. Myasnikov, 'Andrews-Curtis groups' (arXiv 2506.23031, v1 28 June 2025; v2 2 July 2025). The paper studies the full Andrews-Curtis group FAC_k(G) and the natural map to AC_k(G). It shows that for non-elementary torsion-free hyperbolic G (which includes free groups of rank at least 2) the full group acts faithfully on every nontrivial orbit on G^k, so the natural map is an isomorphism. The journal version is in Groups, Complexity, Cryptology 16(1), July 2025.
events.revisions: v2 2 Jul 2025. Journal: Groups, Complexity, Cryptology 16(1) (special issue for Ben Fine), listed July 2025 (search listing).
events.delivers: A structural result about the Andrews-Curtis group, not transitivity. The conjecture for free G of rank k is that AC_k(G) acts transitively on N_k(G); the paper's theorem concerns the full group FAC_k(G) and the isomorphism with AC_k(G), and does not state transitivity.
events.remains: The transitivity statement that the conjecture asserts for free groups; the trivial-group statement.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the special issue
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in volume 16 issue 1 (2025); the referee process was not inspected

events.direction: Structural result on the group version; cuts neither way on transitivity.

events.what_happened: C. Zhang, A. Zhou, R. J. George, S. Gukov, A. Anandkumar, 'AI-Driven Mathematical Discovery for the Andrews-Curtis Conjecture' (NeurIPS 2025 poster, MATH-AI workshop; OpenReview forum lt3Lpa4d2d). The abstract says the authors formalized the conjecture in Lean and built a deterministic autoformalizer, ACC, that checks AC trivialization paths and produces Lean proofs; they benchmark 'state-of-the-art LLM theorem provers' on AC tasks; they use LLMs to extract reusable theorem statements from ACC-generated proofs and add them to reinforcement learning agent training; 'Across all runs, we solved 753 presentations belonging to the Miller-Schupp (MS) family, disproving them as potential counterexamples to the AC conjecture.' The Two-Hump paper calls this 'concurrent work (Zhang et al., 2025)'.
events.revisions: No arXiv version or code link found. The exact month of first public posting is not established, so only the year is given.
events.delivers: Unstable trivializations (with Lean-checked paths, per the abstract) of 753 Miller-Schupp family presentations, counted across all runs (distinct count not stated). The abstract frames these as 'disproving them as potential counterexamples'. Restricted to the MS family.
events.remains: The conjecture for all other presentations and families, and the AK series including AK(3).
events.time_since_posted: about 10 months since the 2025 poster; no independent public check found

machine_checked.system: Lean (the abstract says the conjecture was formalized in Lean and that the autoformalizer produces Lean proofs)

events.directly_checkable: The Lean proofs of the trivialization paths would be the direct check; no repository was found, and the OpenReview page could not be read.
events.doubts: The count is 'across all runs', not clearly distinct presentations. No code, arXiv version or sorry status found. The abstract's LLM role is described as theorem extraction that feeds RL training, and the authors say this increases the number of trivializations; that is the authors' claim, not checked.
events.direction: Trivializations of MS-family instances, claimed as disproving them as potential counterexamples; the conjecture itself is not claimed settled.
events.object: Lean-formalized trivialization paths for 753 Miller-Schupp family presentations (paths generated by the deterministic autoformalizer ACC and by RL agents with LLM-extracted lemmas); the individual presentations and paths were not read.

events.what_happened: J. Carreras, 'Machine-checkable equivalence certificates at the length-14 Andrews-Curtis frontier' (arXiv 2607.23611, v1 26 July 2026; single author; math.GR). Claims four explicit AC-equivalences among six length-14 Miller-Schupp presentations, each given as an elementary-move sequence: classical candidate equivalent to an unresolved MS(2,...) presentation (36 moves); that MS(2,...) equivalent to another MS(2,...) (85 moves); MS(3, yx^2y) equivalent to AK(3) (66 moves); MS(3, y^-1x^2y^-1) equivalent to AK(3) (13 moves). It states that the third and fourth are the first public explicit certificates for AK(3) equivalences that Shehper et al. stated without proof.
events.revisions: v1 only, as of my fetch.
events.delivers: Unstable AC-equivalences among six length-14 presentations: two MS(3)-presentations equivalent to AK(3) (two of the four Shehper et al. claims), and two equivalences among MS(2)-presentations (one of them unresolved before). No presentation is shown trivial. AK(3) is not trivialised.
events.remains: Whether AK(3) and the two MS(2) presentations that the paper leaves unresolved are AC-trivial; AK(3) is the shortest potential counterexample and remains untrivialised; lengths 15 and above.
events.time_since_posted: about 2.5 months (26 July to 11 October 2026); no published reading or review found

machine_checked.system: Custom Python 3 standard-library verifier (ac_verify.py, self-tests selftest_ac.py); not Lean

events.directly_checkable: Each certificate is an explicit elementary-move sequence in the repository; the README says the verifier replays Theorems 1 to 4 in under a minute with only the standard library. The README also says part of the material is outside the trivialisation and equivalence modes and needs a custom endpoint check. I did not run the verifier.
events.doubts: Single author; no journal; no independent replay found; the verifier and the certificates come from the same author. The README notes that the Table-2 analysis needs third-party inputs. Nothing else specific.

events.what_happened: M. Lackenby, 'The stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture and thickenable presentations of the trivial group' (arXiv 2606.06122, submitted 4 June 2026, one version). The abstract says it establishes an explicit upper bound on the number of stable AC moves that convert thickenable balanced presentations of the trivial group to the standard one-generator presentation, and that thickenable balanced presentations 'satisfy the (unstable) Andrews-Curtis conjecture'. A thickenable presentation is one whose 2-complex embeds in a 3-manifold. The result was previously talked about at the Oxford Topology Seminar (18 May 2026, title 'The stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture for thickenable group presentations'), which per the listing says 'for such presentations, the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture is known to hold'. The date is the arXiv write-up, per the rule.
events.revisions: Single version as of my fetch. Seminar talk 18 May 2026 preceded the write-up.
events.delivers: Unstable AC for a restricted class: thickenable balanced presentations of the trivial group (2-complex embeds in a 3-manifold), plus an explicit exponential-type bound on stable moves for that class. The class is the restriction.
events.remains: The unstable conjecture for presentations that are not thickenable, and the conjecture as a whole.
events.time_since_posted: about 4 months (4 June to 11 October 2026); no published reaction found
events.directly_checkable: Membership of a given presentation in the thickenable class (embedding of its 2-complex in a 3-manifold) can be checked per presentation; not checked.
events.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture for the thickenable class; no counterexample; restricted by class.

events.what_happened: L. Fagan, M. Tarquini, A. Shehper, M. Manko, A. Gruen, C. Huang, G. Butbaia, D. Passaro, S. Gukov, 'The Two-Hump Problem: Bridging the Difficulty Gap in Mathematical Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv 2606.21611, submitted 19 June 2026; ICML 2026, PMLR 306, per the arXiv comment). It identifies a 'Two-Hump' difficulty distribution in AC instances; introduces supermoves, data generation and Transformer-based architectures; a PPO agent 'solves 153 more presentations than the prior baseline (610 vs 457)'; it releases AC-19 (125,192 AC-trivial presentations of length at most 19) and AC-1M (over one million harder examples). It says AK(1) and AK(2) are trivializable and that AK(n) for n of at least 3 remains open, with AK(3) 'beyond current reach'. Section 1.1 says it trivializes 'over 100 previously unsolved presentations from a standard benchmark' from the Miller-Schupp family, described as 'a famous two-parameter family of potential counterexamples'. The paper's own framing is that AC is 'an illustrative example' for ML.
events.revisions: Single arXiv version (v1). Accepted at ICML 2026 per the comment field.
events.delivers: Unstable computational trivializations of specific benchmark presentations (instances; the benchmark mixes MS-family presentations and other AC-trivial presentations). The abstract and introduction do not claim a new result about the conjecture itself. Counts are presentations solved, not families resolved.

events.what_happened: Bar-Ilan University Laboratory for AI in Algebra (page last updated 09/02/2026 on the page's own stamp, which is ambiguous between 9 February and 2 September 2026). Under 'Searching for counterexamples to the Andrews-Curtis conjecture', the page says: 'Assisted by AI tools, we construct such images and explore the corresponding finite Andrews-Curtis graphs to search for short trivialization sequences'. The 'images' are homomorphic images of Akbulut-Kirby presentations in finite groups of Lie type over finite fields. The page says the work is joint with Alexei Miasnikov (Stevens) and directed by Elena Bunina. It states no result.

disputes.summary: The stable-triviality claim for an Akbulut-Kirby candidate in the v1 abstract of arXiv 2408.15332 (27 Aug 2024) is not in the v2 abstract (11 Feb 2025). The v2 introduction says a misprint in MMS02 p.10 undermines the claim that presentation (1) is stably AC-trivial, and treats AK(3) as a potential counterexample to the stable conjecture. Lisitsa's arXiv 2501.18601 (17 Jan 2025) and the 2026 Carreras paper and press treat AK(3) as stably AC-trivial or stably AC-equivalent to the trivial presentation, attributing this to Shehper et al. (2024). The two readings are not reconciled in the sources I read; Lisitsa's sequences are an independent route if they check.

Caltech PMA (13 Feb 2025) says the team 'used AI to solve two families of problems within the Andrews-Curtis conjecture' and 'disproved families of problems, referred to as potential counterexamples'; it states that the main conjecture was not solved. The Scientific American article (11 Aug 2025) says 'Using the agentic AI system, the team was able to solve large families of longstanding potential counterexamples', and that the conjecture 'has never been proved or disproved'; it names no AI system for the Andrews-Curtis work (it names AlphaGo, AlphaStar, OpenAI's GPT and xAI's Grok only as background). The AI Man blog (12 Aug 2025) headlines 'AI Cracks 60-Year Old Math Mystery' but its body says the AI 'didn't solve the whole conjecture'. The authors' own account describes a machine-learning algorithm and reinforcement learning.

The 2025 talk by Bagherifard with Eftekhary (Oregon, 12 May 2025; Georgia Tech, 6 Dec 2025) says a 'version of the conjecture is not true', while their 2022 preprint is about a 3-manifold analogue and states only that the analogue fails for some simple balanced 3-manifolds. Which version the talk means is not stated; no written argument was found.

Shehper et al. (v2 Section 3.3) claim four Miller-Schupp presentations are AC-equivalent to AK(3); Carreras (2026) says these were stated without published move sequences and certifies two of them (MS(3,...), 66 and 13 moves). The other two claimed equivalences have no sequence in the sources I read.

Counts of Miller-Schupp presentations are reported in three places on different bases: 753 'across all runs' (Zhang et al. 2025, NeurIPS abstract, distinct count not stated); 'hundreds' in Shehper et al. (v2 Section 1); and 'over 100 previously unsolved presentations' (Two-Hump, Section 1.1). Whether these overlap is not established.

summary: Read against the statement, the unstable conjecture is unresolved: no source claims a proof or a counterexample to the trivial-group claim. The events since January 2024 fall into four kinds. (1) Instance-level computer-assisted trivializations of Miller-Schupp family presentations: Lisitsa's May 2024 automated-theorem-proving preprint (n = 3..7; the journal reports 3..8, not read), Shehper et al. v2 (hundreds of MS presentations, three infinite subfamilies, per the abstract), Zhang et al. NeurIPS 2025 (753 MS presentations across all runs, with Lean paths per the abstract), and Two-Hump, June 2026 (over 100 newly trivialized benchmark presentations; 610 vs 457 PPO solves). These are instances of a universal claim; I have recorded them without deciding whether they move the conjecture's quantity. (2) Reductions and equivalences involving AK(3) and the AK series: Shehper et al. v2 (length reduction for all but two AK series presentations; four MS presentations claimed AC-equivalent to AK(3)), and Carreras (July 2026), who certifies two of those claims with explicit sequences and finds two further equivalences among MS(2) presentations, without trivializing AK(3). AK(3) is stated open for the unstable question by Shehper v2 and by Two-Hump. (3) A stable-version AK(3) result that is contested: the v1 abstract (Aug 2024) claims an Akbulut-Kirby candidate is stably AC-trivial; the v2 text (Feb 2025) attributes the stable claim for presentation (1) to a misprint in the 2002 Myasnikov-Myasnikov-Shpilrain paper; Lisitsa's January 2025 Prover9 proof independently asserts stable AC-equivalence of AK(3) to the trivial presentation; I did not check Lisitsa's sequences. Fagan-Qiu-Wang (Dec 2024, v2 Jan 2026) reduce the stable conjecture to fake surfaces and prove the complexity-below-6 case, which is partial stable progress. (4) An unstable proof for a restricted class: Lackenby (June 2026) shows thickenable balanced presentations satisfy the unstable conjecture and gives a stable move bound for them; no reaction found. The 2025 Bagherifard-Eftekhary talks claim 'a version of the conjecture is not true', but the abstract does not say which version and no written argument was found; the 2022 paper they cite concerns a 3-manifold analogue. Barmak (AGT 2025) disproves a generalised equivalence for presentations of Z x Z, not the trivial-group statement. Gilman-Myasnikov (2025) prove a structural result for the Andrews-Curtis group that does not address transitivity. Historic results from 2003 to 2021 are recorded as events, including a withdrawn 2021 disproof of a relative version. AI involvement: the 2024-2026 computational work uses reinforcement learning (Shehper et al.; Two-Hump, PPO), LLM-extracted lemmas feeding RL training (Zhang et al.), a probabilistic automaton classifier with automated reasoning (Fairbank et al.), and classical automated theorem proving (Lisitsa, Prover9), which I treat as not an AI system under the record's definition but recorded as named. Carreras and Lackenby disclose no AI use. The Bar-Ilan lab page says 'Assisted by AI tools' with no named system and no result. I found no Claude or Anthropic involvement. The Caltech press and the Scientific American piece describe an 'agentic AI system' that is not named in the sources I could read. Close calls: whether the stable AK(3) result counts for the unstable question (it does not, on the statement); whether 753 or the Two-Hump counts move a quantity the conjecture names (I read them as instance counts); whether the RL and classifier systems are AI systems in the sense the project uses (I recorded them as AI, with the method named).
competing_reading: The strongest case for a larger effect: the NeurIPS 2025 abstract says LLM-extracted theorems were added to RL training and that this raised trivialization counts, which is the most direct case of an authors' account crediting an LLM with load-bearing mathematics; the Caltech press calls the work AI-driven; and the Shehper v1 claim, if it stands, would make AK(3) stably trivial, which for a stable-version bullet would be a resolution of the candidate most experts regard as the main counterexample. The strongest case for a smaller effect: the unstable statement quantifies over all balanced presentations, and every event above is an instance, a stable-form result, a class restriction, or an equivalence between presentations; no event trivializes AK(3) or any family in the unstable setting; the stable AK(3) claim is contested by the authors' own v2; and the 753 and 610 counts are cumulative or benchmark-relative.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The Shehper et al. v2 changelog and Appendix F (the MMS02 misprint), to see whether the stable AK(3) claim is withdrawn or still asserted through another route; and an independent replay of Lisitsa's Prover9-derived sequences for AK(3). (b) The body of the NeurIPS 2025 paper (OpenReview PDF or an arXiv version): the exact sentence on the LLM role, whether 753 is distinct, the Lean repository, and a grep for sorry. (c) The Fairbank-Lisitsa-Vernitski results section (not readable here; the Springer page redirected to a login). (d) The Lackenby full text and any reaction, and whether AK(3) is thickenable. (e) Replay of Carreras's four certificates with the repository verifier, and whether the two AK(3) equivalences are the same ones Shehper claimed. (f) The identity of the 'second preprint' the Caltech press (13 Feb 2025) mentions, which reports solving more families of potential counterexamples. (g) Whether the Bagherifard-Eftekhary 'version is not true' claim has a written argument and which version it concerns.

event.what_happened: A. Shehper, A. Medina-Mardones, L. Fagan, B. Lewandowski, A. Gruen, Y. Qiu, P. Kucharski, Z. Wang, S. Gukov, 'What makes math problems hard for reinforcement learning: a case study' (arXiv 2408.15332, v1 27 Aug 2024; v2 11 Feb 2025). v1 abstract: the authors 'demonstrate that one of the potential counterexamples due to Akbulut and Kirby, whose status escaped direct mathematical methods for 39 years, is stably AC-trivial'. v2 abstract, read directly: length reducibility of all but two presentations in the Akbulut-Kirby series (1981), and resolution of various potential counterexamples in the Miller-Schupp series (1991), including three infinite subfamilies. The v2 introduction says 'we also found AC-trivializations of hundreds of Miller-Schupp presentations' and 'we apply reinforcement learning to demonstrate its AC equivalence to AK(3)'. v2 Section 2 says 'the presentation MS(3,w1) of length 15 is AC-equivalent to AK(3)', and Section 3.3 says four presentations 'are AC-equivalent to AK(3)'. v2 Section 2 says the AK(3) trivialization attempts by breadth-first search failed and calls AK(3) a potential counterexample.
event.revisions: v1 27 Aug 2024 abstract claims stable AC-triviality of an Akbulut-Kirby candidate (the abstract does not name it; the 39-year gap matches AK(3)). v2 11 Feb 2025: the abstract no longer contains that claim; the v2 introduction says 'we discovered a subtle misprint in [MMS02, p.10] that had gone unnoticed for more than 20 years. This misprint undermines the claim that (1) is stably AC-trivial', where (1) is a presentation from the 2002 paper and the paper says (1) is AC-equivalent to AK(3). Appendix F ('A misprint in the Wirtinger presentation of [MMS02]') is listed but was not readable. v2 Section 9 calls AK(3) 'a potential counterexample for the stable Andrews-Curtis conjecture'. I did not see an explicit retraction sentence and did not see a changelog.
event.delivers: Unstable, restricted to the Akbulut-Kirby series and Miller-Schupp families: length reduction for the AK series (all but two presentations); AC-equivalences of several Miller-Schupp presentations to AK(3) (including a length-15 example and four presentations per Section 3.3); unstable trivializations of hundreds of Miller-Schupp presentations and of three infinite subfamilies of potential counterexamples (abstract; instance-level, not a proof for the full families as far as I read). The v1 stable-triviality claim for an AK-type candidate is not delivered in v2 and is in any case about the stable question.
event.remains: The unstable conjecture for AK(n) with n of at least 3 (AK(3) is stated open in v2 Section 2 and in the Two-Hump paper); the unstable status of all Miller-Schupp presentations not listed; the stable question, where v2 says AK(3) remains a potential counterexample.

judgement.why: The statement is the unstable conjecture for all balanced presentations of the trivial group. Stable-form results (Lisitsa 2025, Fagan-Qiu-Wang), other groups or relations (Barmak, Gilman-Myasnikov), 3-manifold analogues and the withdrawn Metzler paper are variants. Finite lists of trivialized presentations (Myasnikov 2003, Lisitsa 2024, Zhang et al., Two-Hump) are instances. Carreras gives equivalences between presentations, not trivializations, so it settles nothing (none). Lackenby proves the unstable conjecture for the thickenable class: a case. Shehper et al. was the close call. Its abstract claims to resolve three infinite Miller-Schupp subfamilies, which is a class restriction and so a case and not just instances. I marked it doubtful because the record did not check that claim against the body and because the authors dropped their v1 stable claim. I scored its AI role as assisted rather than generated: the RL agent found the move sequences, but extending them to infinite families looks like human work. For Zhang et al. and Two-Hump, the RL agents produced the trivializing paths themselves, so they are generated, though both are discarded as instances.
judgement.doubts: The Shehper 'three infinite subfamilies' claim was taken from the v2 abstract only. If those are really just instance lists, the event's scope should be instances. Whether RL agents count as AI systems is taken on the record's framing.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
